questions.question: A chemical reaction is carried out in a sealed steel container. The steel container allows heat transfer, and the temperature of the container changes during the reaction. Which statement best describes this thermodynamic system?
options: Matter flows freely across the boundary, but energy exchange is restricted.
Energy is exchanged with the surroundings, but matter is contained within the system.
Neither matter nor energy can cross the boundaries of the system.
The system boundary is imaginary, allowing both matter and energy exchange.
questions.explanation: B is correct because a 'sealed' container implies no matter can enter or leave the system. A 'conducting material' that allows 'heat transfer' means energy can be exchanged with the surroundings. This combination defines a closed system. A is wrong as it describes an open system with restricted energy. C is wrong as it describes an isolated system. D is wrong because a system always has a boundary, real or imaginary, and this scenario is a closed system, not necessarily an open one by default.
questions.hint: Analyze the implications of a 'sealed' container and a 'conducting material' for matter and energy exchange.

questions.question: When studying a chemical reaction occurring within a test tube, the most appropriate definition for the 'surroundings' in a practical thermodynamic context would be:
options: The entire universe excluding the test tube and its contents.
Only the immediate region of space around the test tube that can interact with it.
The internal walls of the test tube forming the boundary.
Any external heat source or sink, ignoring the air in the room.
questions.explanation: B is correct. While theoretically the surroundings are the entire universe other than the system, for practical purposes, the surroundings are defined as that portion of the remaining universe which can interact with the system. This usually refers to the region of space in the neighborhood of the system. A is wrong as it represents the theoretical definition, not the practical one. C is wrong because the internal walls of the test tube would be considered the boundary, not the surroundings. D is wrong because the surroundings include all interacting elements, not just specific heat sources or sinks.
questions.hint: Recall the distinction made between the entire universe as surroundings and the 'practical' definition for analysis.

topic: Thermodynamic Systems, State Variables, and Internal Energy

questions.question: Which of the following statements accurately defines an isolated system in thermodynamics?
options: Exchanges only energy with the surroundings.
Exchanges both energy and matter with the surroundings.
Exchanges only matter with the surroundings.
Exchanges neither energy nor matter with the surroundings.
questions.explanation: D is correct because an isolated system, by definition, has no exchange of either energy or matter with its surroundings. A is incorrect as it describes a closed system where matter is not exchanged but energy can be. B is incorrect as it describes an open system. C is incorrect; a system exchanging only matter would still exchange energy, thus not being isolated.
questions.hint: Recall the distinct classifications of thermodynamic systems based on their interaction with surroundings.
questions.ncertPara: 3. Isolated System In an isolated system, there is no exchange of energy or matter between the system and the surroundings [Fig. 5.2 (c)]. The presence of reactants in a thermos flask or any other closed insulated vessel is an example of an isolated system. 5.1.3 The State of the System The system must be described in order to make any useful calculations by specifying quantitatively each of the properties such as its pressure (p), volume (V), and temperature (T ) as well as the composition of the system. We need to describe the system by specifying it before and after the change. You would recall from your Physics course that the state of a system in mechanics is completely specified at a given instant of time, by the position and velocity of each mass point of the system. In thermodynamics, a different and much simpler concept of the state of a system is introduced. It does not need detailed knowledge of motion of each particle because, we deal with average measurable properties of the system. We specify the state of the system by state functions or state variables. The state of a thermodynamic system is described by its measurable or macroscopic (bulk) properties. We can describe the state of a gas by quoting its pressure (p), volume (V), temperature (T ), amount (n) etc. Variables like p, V, T are called state variables or state functions because their values depend only on the state of the system and not on how it is reached. In order to completely define the state of a system it is not necessary to define all the properties of the system; as only a certain number of properties can be varied independently. This number depends on the nature of the system. Once these minimum number of macroscopic properties are fixed, others automatically have definite values. The state of the surroundings can never be completely specified; fortunately it is not necessary to do so. 5.1.4 The Internal Energy as a State Function When we talk about our chemical system losing or gaining energy, we need to introduce

questions.question: Which of the following thermodynamic properties is NOT a state function?
options: Pressure (p)
Volume (V)
Temperature (T)
Heat (q)
questions.explanation: D is correct because heat (q) is a path function; its value depends on the specific path followed during a process, not solely on the initial and final states. Pressure (p), Volume (V), and Temperature (T) are all state functions, as explicitly mentioned in thermodynamics, meaning their values are fixed once the state of the system is defined, irrespective of how that state was achieved.
questions.hint: Recall that state functions depend only on the initial and final states, not the path taken.

questions.question: The internal energy ($U$) of a thermodynamic system can change due to which of the following interactions with its surroundings?
options: Only when heat passes into or out of the system.
Only when work is done on or by the system.
Only when matter enters or leaves the system.
When heat passes, work is done, or matter enters/leaves the system.
questions.explanation: D is correct because the internal energy ($U$) of a system can change when heat passes into or out of the system, when work is done on or by the system, or when matter enters or leaves the system. Options A, B, and C are incorrect because they list only one or two out of the three possible ways for internal energy to change, presenting an incomplete picture.
questions.hint: Consider all fundamental ways a system can interact with its surroundings to alter its total energy content.

questions.question: Which characteristic specifically defines an adiabatic process?
options: Constant temperature throughout the process.
No change in pressure between the system and surroundings.
No transfer of heat between the system and surroundings.
No work done on or by the system.
questions.explanation: C is correct because an adiabatic process is explicitly defined as one where there is no transfer of heat between the system and surroundings. A is incorrect as constant temperature defines an isothermal process. B is incorrect as pressure can change during an adiabatic process. D is incorrect as work can be done on or by the system during an adiabatic process.
questions.hint: Focus on the type of exchange that is prevented in an adiabatic system.
questions.ncertPara: a quantity which represents the total energy of the system. It may be chemical, electrical, mechanical or any other type of energy you may think of, the sum of all these is the energy of the system. In thermodynamics, we call it the internal energy, U of the system, which may change, when • heat passes into or out of the system, • work is done on or by the system, • matter enters or leaves the system. These systems are classified accordingly as you have already studied in section 5.1.2. (a) Work Let us first examine a change in internal energy by doing work. We take a system containing some quantity of water in a thermos flask or in an insulated beaker. This would not allow exchange of heat between the system and surroundings through its boundary and we call this type of system as adiabatic. The manner in which the state of such a system may be changed will be called adiabatic process. Adiabatic process is a process in which there is no transfer of heat between the system and surroundings. Here, the wall separating the system and the surroundings is called the adiabatic wall (Fig. 5.3).

questions.question: Which of the following scenarios best represents an isolated system?
options: Hot coffee in an open cup.
Water in a sealed, non-insulated bottle.
Reactants in a thermos flask.
A balloon filled with air at room temperature.
questions.explanation: C) Reactants in a thermos flask. In an isolated system, there is no exchange of energy or matter between the system and the surroundings. A thermos flask or a closed insulated vessel is an example of an isolated system because it prevents matter from leaving or entering and minimizes heat transfer through its insulated walls. Option A represents an open system, which exchanges both energy and matter. Options B and D represent closed systems, which allow energy exchange through their boundaries but do not allow matter exchange.

We can describe the state of a gas by quoting its pressure (p), volume (V), temperature (T ), amount (n) etc. Variables like p, V, T are called state variables or state functions because their values depend only on the state of the system and not on how it is reached. In order to completely define the state of a system it is not necessary to define all the properties of the system; as only a certain number of properties can be varied independently. This number depends on the nature of the system. Once these minimum number of macroscopic properties are fixed, others automatically have definite values. The state of the surroundings can never be completely specified; fortunately it is not necessary to do so. 5.1.4 The Internal Energy as a State Function When we talk about our chemical system losing or gaining energy, we need to introduce

a quantity which represents the total energy of the system. It may be chemical, electrical, mechanical or any other type of energy you may think of, the sum of all these is the energy of the system. In thermodynamics, we call it the internal energy, U of the system, which may change, when • heat passes into or out of the system, • work is done on or by the system, • matter enters or leaves the system. Adiabatic process is a process in which there is no transfer of heat between the system and surroundings. Here, the wall separating the system and the surroundings is called the adiabatic wall (Fig. 5.3).

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes a state function in thermodynamics?
options: Its value depends on the path taken to reach a particular state.
Its change in value depends only on the initial and final states of the system.
It is always equal to the heat exchanged with the surroundings.
It is always equal to the work done on or by the system.
questions.explanation: B is correct because a state function is a thermodynamic property whose value depends only on the current state of the system, not on the path taken to reach that state. Therefore, the change in a state function depends only on the initial and final states. A is wrong because this describes a path function (like work or heat). C is wrong because a state function is a property of the system, not necessarily equal to heat, which is a form of energy transfer and a path function. D is wrong because a state function is not always equal to work, which is also a form of energy transfer and a path function.
questions.hint: Recall that a state function's value depends solely on the state of the system, not how that state was achieved.
questions.ncertPara: One way: We do some mechanical work, say 1 kJ, by rotating a set of small paddles and thereby churning water. Let the new state be called B state and its temperature, as TB. It is found that TB > TA and the change in temperature, ∆T = TB–TA. Let the internal energy of the system in state B be UB and the change in internal energy, ∆U =UB– UA. Second way: We now do an equal amount (i.e., 1kJ) electrical work with the help of an immersion rod and note down the temperature change. We find that the change in temperature is same as in the earlier case, say, TB – TA. In fact, the experiments in the above manner were done by J. P. Joule between 1840–50 and he was able to show that a given amount of work done on the system, no matter how it was done (irrespective of path) produced the same change of state, as measured by the change in the temperature of the system. questions.question: According to IUPAC conventions in chemical thermodynamics, what is the sign of work ($w_{ad}$) when work is done by the system on the surroundings?
options: Positive, and internal energy increases.
Negative, and internal energy increases.
Positive, and internal energy decreases.
Negative, and internal energy decreases.
questions.explanation: D is correct because, by IUPAC convention, when work is done by the system on the surroundings, $w_{ad}$ is negative, which corresponds to a decrease in the internal energy of the system. A is wrong because positive work is done on the system, increasing internal energy. B is wrong because negative work is done by the system, but internal energy decreases, not increases. C is wrong because positive work is done on the system, and it increases internal energy.

questions.question: A chemical system absorbs $5\ kJ$ of heat from its surroundings at constant volume. According to IUPAC convention, what is the sign and value of 'q' for this process?
options: $q = +5\ kJ$, but $\Delta U$ decreases.
questions.explanation: B is correct because, according to IUPAC conventions, heat absorbed by the system from the surroundings is considered positive. Thus, for $5\ kJ$ absorbed, $q = +5\ kJ$. A is wrong because heat absorbed is positive, not negative. C is wrong because heat is transferred, so 'q' cannot be zero. D is wrong because while $q = +5\ kJ$ is correct, heat absorbed increases the internal energy, it does not decrease it.
questions.hint: Remember the IUPAC sign convention for heat transfer between system and surroundings.

questions.question: Which of the following sets contains only state functions?
options: Internal energy (U), Work (w), Pressure (p)
Heat (q), Volume (V), Temperature (T)
Internal energy (U), Pressure (p), Temperature (T)

questions.question: For a thermodynamic process occurring at constant volume where no non-PV work is involved, the change in internal energy ($\Delta U$) is equal to:
options: The work done on the system.
The heat transferred to the system.
The sum of work done and heat transferred.
Always zero.
questions.explanation: B is correct. The text states, 'change in internal energy, $\Delta U = q$, when no work is done at constant volume.' This means that under constant volume conditions with no other forms of work, any change in internal energy is solely due to the heat transferred. A is wrong because $\Delta U$ is equal to work done only in an adiabatic process ($q=0$). C is wrong because the sum of work and heat is for a general process, not specifically for constant volume with no work. D is wrong because $\Delta U$ is generally not zero unless it's a cyclic process or an isolated system.
questions.hint: Consider the First Law of Thermodynamics and the implications of a constant volume process.

topic: First Law of Thermodynamics and Internal Energy

questions.question: A chemical system absorbs $15\ J$ of heat from its surroundings and simultaneously $5\ J$ of work is done *on* the system. What is the change in the internal energy ($ÎU$) of the system?
questions.explanation: According to the First Law of Thermodynamics, $ÎU = q + w$. Given that heat is absorbed by the system, $q = +15\ J$. Work is done on the system, so $w = +5\ J$. Therefore, $ÎU = (+15\ J) + (+5\ J) = +20\ J$. Option A is incorrect because it implies $ÎU = q - w$. Option C and D are incorrect as they involve incorrect signs for $q$ or $w$, leading to different magnitudes or signs.
questions.hint: Recall the mathematical statement of the First Law of Thermodynamics, $ÎU = q + w$, and pay close attention to the sign conventions for heat absorbed by the system and work done on the system.
questions.ncertPara: Problem 5.1 Express the change in internal energy of a system when (i) No heat is absorbed by the system from the surroundings, but work (w) is done on the system. What type of wall does the system have ? (ii) No work is done on the system, but q amount of heat is taken out from the system and given to the surroundings. What type of wall does the system have? (iii) w amount of work is done by the system and q amount of heat is supplied to the system. What type of system would it be?

questions.question: A thermodynamic system undergoes a change from an initial State X to a final State Y via two different paths. For Path I, the system absorbs $50\ kJ$ of heat and performs $20\ kJ$ of work on the surroundings. For Path II, the system performs $30\ kJ$ of work on the surroundings. What is the heat exchanged by the system for Path II?
questions.explanation: For Path I, $q_{1} = +50\ kJ$ (heat absorbed). Work done by the system on surroundings means $w_{1} = -20\ kJ$. Using the First Law, $ÎU_{1} = q_{1} + w_{1} = (+50\ kJ) + (-20\ kJ) = +30\ kJ$. Since $ÎU$ is a state function, the change in internal energy for Path II ($ÎU_{2}$) must be the same as for Path I, so $ÎU_{2} = +30\ kJ$. For Path II, work done by the system is $30\ kJ$, so $w_{2} = -30\ kJ$. Applying the First Law for Path II: $ÎU_{2} = q_{2} + w_{2}$. So, $+30\ kJ = q_{2} + (-30\ kJ)$. Rearranging gives $q_{2} = +30\ kJ + 30\ kJ = +60\ kJ$. This means the system absorbs $60\ kJ$ of heat in Path II. Options B, C, and D result from incorrect application of sign conventions or the assumption that $q$ or $w$ are state functions.
questions.hint: Remember that the change in internal energy ($ÎU$) is a state function, meaning it depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path taken. Apply the First Law of Thermodynamics, $ÎU = q + w$, carefully noting the sign conventions for work done by the system.
questions.ncertPara: (c) The general case Let us consider the general case in which a change of state is brought about both by doing work and by transfer of heat. We write change in internal energy for this case as: ∆U = q + w (5.1) For a given change in state, q and w can vary depending on how the change is carried out. However, q +w = ∆U will depend only on initial and final state. It will be independent of the way the change is carried out. If there is no transfer of energy as heat or as work (isolated system) i.e., if w = 0 and q = 0, then ∆ U = 0. The equation 5.1 i.e., ∆U = q + w is mathematical statement of the first law of thermodynamics, which states that The energy of an isolated system is constant. It is commonly stated as the law of conservation of energy i.e., energy can neither be created nor be destroyed. Note: There is considerable difference between the character of the thermodynamic property energy and that of a mechanical property such as volume. We can specify an unambiguous (absolute) value for volume of a system in a particular state, but not the absolute value of the internal energy. However, we can measure only the changes in the internal energy, ∆U of the system.

questions.question: If a thermodynamic system is perfectly isolated from its surroundings, what is the change in its internal energy ($ÎU$)?
options: Positive, as energy is conserved.
Negative, as no energy exchange occurs.
Zero, as both heat and work exchanges are absent.
Dependent on the process carried out.
questions.explanation: An isolated system is defined as one that cannot exchange either energy (heat or work) or matter with its surroundings. Therefore, for an isolated system, $q = 0$ (no heat exchange) and $w = 0$ (no work exchange). According to the First Law of Thermodynamics, $ÎU = q + w$. Substituting $q=0$ and $w=0$, we get $ÎU = 0$. Option A and B are incorrect as the internal energy of an isolated system remains constant, implying zero change. Option D is incorrect because for an isolated system, the change in internal energy is unequivocally zero, independent of any internal processes.
questions.hint: Recall the definition of an isolated system and how it affects the heat and work exchange with the surroundings. Then apply the First Law of Thermodynamics ($ÎU = q + w$).
questions.ncertPara: Problem 5.1 Express the change in internal energy of a system when (i) No heat is absorbed by the system from the surroundings, but work (w) is done on the system. What type of wall does the system have ? (ii) No work is done on the system, but q amount of heat is taken out from the system and given to the surroundings. What type of wall does the system have? (iii) w amount of work is done by the system and q amount of heat is supplied to the system. What type of system would it be?

questions.question: In an adiabatic process, $200\ J$ of work is done *by* the system on the surroundings. What is the change in internal energy ($ÎU$) of the system?
options: Cannot be determined without heat information.
questions.explanation: An adiabatic process is characterized by no heat exchange with the surroundings, meaning $q = 0$. According to the First Law of Thermodynamics, $ÎU = q + w$. Substituting $q=0$, we get $ÎU = w$. Work done *by* the system on the surroundings is conventionally assigned a negative sign. Given that $200\ J$ of work is done *by* the system, $w = -200\ J$. Therefore, $ÎU = -200\ J$. Option A is incorrect due to a sign error. Option C would only be true for an isolated system where both heat and work are zero. Option D is incorrect because for an adiabatic process, the change in internal energy is solely determined by the work done.
questions.hint: Recall that for an adiabatic process, there is no heat exchange ($q=0$). The sign convention for work done *by* the system must be correctly applied in the First Law of Thermodynamics ($ÎU = q + w$).
questions.ncertPara: Problem 5.1 Express the change in internal energy of a system when (i) No heat is absorbed by the system from the surroundings, but work (w) is done on the system. What type of wall does the system have ? (ii) No work is done on the system, but q amount of heat is taken out from the system and given to the surroundings. What type of wall does the system have? (iii) w amount of work is done by the system and q amount of heat is supplied to the system. What type of system would it be?

questions.question: A chemical reaction occurs in a closed system. The system releases $30\ kJ$ of heat to the surroundings and simultaneously does $10\ kJ$ of work on the surroundings. What is the change in internal energy ($ÎU$) for the system?
questions.explanation: According to the First Law of Thermodynamics, $ÎU = q + w$. In this scenario, the system releases $30\ kJ$ of heat, which means $q = -30\ kJ$ (negative because heat leaves the system). The system does $10\ kJ$ of work on the surroundings, which means $w = -10\ kJ$ (negative because the system expends energy to do work). Substituting these values into the First Law equation: $ÎU = (-30\ kJ) + (-10\ kJ) = -40\ kJ$. Options A, B, and C result from incorrect sign conventions for heat released or work done by the system.
questions.hint: Carefully apply the First Law of Thermodynamics ($ÎU = q + w$). Remember that heat released by the system is negative ($q<0$), and work done *by* the system on the surroundings is negative ($w<0$).

(iii) w amount of work is done by the system and q amount of heat is supplied to the system. What type of system would it be?

Note: There is considerable difference between the character of the thermodynamic property energy and that of a mechanical property such as volume. We can specify an unambiguous (absolute) value for volume of a system in a particular state, but not the absolute value of the internal energy. However, we can measure only the changes in the internal energy, ∆U of the system.

But most of chemical reactions are carried out not at constant volume, but in flasks or test tubes under constant atmospheric pressure. We need to define another state function which may be suitable under these conditions. We may write equation (5.1) as ∆U = qp – p∆V at constant pressure, where qp is heat absorbed by the system and –p ∆V represent expansion work done by the system. Let us represent the initial state by subscript 1 and final state by 2 We can rewrite the above equation as U2–U1 = qp – p (V2 – V1) On rearranging, we get (5.6) qp = (U2 + pV2) – (U1 + pV1) Now we can define another thermodynamic function, the enthalpy H [Greek word enthalpien, to warm or heat content] as : H = U + pV (5.7) so, equation (5.6) becomes qp= H2 – H1 = ∆H Although q is a path dependent function, H is a state function because it depends on U, p and V, all of which are state functions. Therefore, ∆H is independent of path. Hence, qp is also independent of path. For finite changes at constant pressure, we can write equation 5.7 as ∆H = ∆U + ∆pV Since p is constant, we can write ∆H = ∆U + p∆V (5.8) It is important to note that when heat is absorbed by the system at constant pressure, we are actually measuring changes in the enthalpy.

Remember ∆H = qp, heat absorbed by the system at constant pressure. ∆H is negative for exothermic reactions which evolve heat during the reaction and ∆H is positive for endothermic reactions which absorb heat from the surroundings. At constant volume (∆V = 0), ∆U = qV, therefore equation 5.8 becomes ∆H = ∆U = qV The difference between ∆H and ∆U is not usually significant for systems consisting of only solids and / or liquids. = 37.904 kJ mol–1 (b) Extensive and Intensive Properties In thermodynamics, a distinction is made between extensive properties and intensive properties. An extensive property is a property whose value depends on the quantity or size of matter present in the system. For example, mass, volume, internal energy, enthalpy, heat capacity, etc. are extensive properties. Those properties which do not depend on the quantity or size of matter present are known as intensive properties. For example temperature, density, pressure etc. are intensive properties. A molar property, χm, is the value of an extensive property χ of the system for 1 mol of the substance. If n is  the amount of matter,  m  n is independent of the amount of matter. Other examples are molar volume, Vm and molar heat capacity, C m . Let us understand the distinction between extensive and intensive properties by considering a gas enclosed in a container of volume V and at temperature T [Fig. 5.6(a)]. Let us make a partition such that volume is halved, each part [Fig. 5.6 (b)] now has one half of the original volume, V , but the temperature will still remain the same i.e., T. It is clear that volume is an extensive property and temperature is an intensive property.

Amount of heat required to vaporize one mole of a liquid at constant temperature and under standard pressure (1bar) is called its standard enthalpy of vaporization or molar enthalpy of vaporization, ∆vapH . Sublimation is direct conversion of a solid into its vapour. Solid CO2 or ‘dry ice’ sublimes at 195K with ∆subH=25.2 kJ mol–1; naphthalene sublimes slowly and for this ∆sub H = 73.0 kJ mol–1 . Standard enthalpy of sublimation, ∆subH is the change in enthalpy when one mole of a solid substance sublimes at a constant temperature and under standard pressure (1bar). The magnitude of the enthalpy change depends on the strength of the intermolecular interactions in the substance undergoing the phase transfomations. For example, the strong hydrogen bonds between water molecules hold them tightly in liquid phase. For an organic liquid, such as acetone, the intermolecular dipole-dipole interactions are significantly weaker. Thus, it requires less heat to vaporise 1 mol of acetone than it does to vaporize 1 mol of water. Table 5.1 gives values of standard enthalpy changes of fusion and vaporisation for some substances. The reference state of an element is its most stable state of aggregation at 25°C and 1 bar pressure. For example, the reference state of dihydrogen is H 2 gas and those of dioxygen, carbon and sulphur are O2 gas, Cgraphite and Srhombic respectively. Some reactions with standard molar enthalpies of formation are as follows.

paragraphs.text: H2(g) + ½O2 (g) → H2O(1); ∆f H = –285.8 kJ mol–1 C (graphite, s) + 2H2(g) → Ch4 (g); ∆f H = –74.81 kJ mol–1 2C (graphite, s)+3H2 (g)+ ½O2(g) → C2H5OH(1); ∆f H  = – 277.7kJ mol–1 It is important to understand that a standard molar enthalpy of formation, ∆f H , is just a special case of ∆rH , where one mole of a compound is formed from its constituent elements, as in the above three equations, where 1 mol of each, water, methane and ethanol is formed. In contrast, the enthalpy change for an exothermic reaction: CaO(s) + CO2(g) → CaCo3(s); ∆rH  = – 178.3kJ mol–1 is not an enthalpy of formation of calcium carbonate, since calcium carbonate has been formed from other compounds, and not from its constituent elements. Also, for the reaction given below, enthalpy change is not standard enthalpy of formation, ∆fH  for HBr(g). H2(g) + Br2(l) → 2HBr(g); ∆r H  = – 178.3kJ mol–1

Here two moles, instead of one mole of the product is formed from the elements, i.e., ∆r H  = 2∆f H Therefore, by dividing all coefficients in the balanced equation by 2, expression for enthalpy of formation of HBr (g) is written as ½H2(g) + ½Br2(1) → HBr(g); ∆f H = – 36.4 kJ mol–1 Standard enthalpies of formation of some common substances are given in Table 5.2. By convention, standard enthalpy for formation, ∆f H , of an element in reference state, i.e., its most stable state of aggregation is taken as zero. Suppose, you are a chemical engineer and want to know how much heat is required to decompose calcium carbonate to lime and carbon dioxide, with all the substances in their standard state. CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g); ∆r H = ?

Here, we can make use of standard enthalpy of formation and calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction. The following general equation can be used for the enthalpy change calculation. ∆rH = ∑ ai ∆f H (products) – ∑ bi ∆f H (reactants) i i (5.15) where a and b represent the coefficients of the products and reactants in the balanced equation. Let us apply the above equation for decomposition of calcium carbonate. Here, coefficients ‘a’ and ‘b’ are 1 each. Therefore, ∆rH = ∆f H  = [CaO(s)]+ ∆f H  [CO2(g)] – ∆f H  = [CaCO3(s)] =1 (–635.1 kJ mol–1) + 1(–393.5 kJ mol–1) –1(–1206.9 kJ mol–1) –1 = 178.3 kJ mol Thus, the decomposition of CaCO3 (s) is an endothermic process and you have to heat it for getting the desired products. (d) Thermochemical Equations A balanced chemical equation together with the value of its ∆rH is called a thermochemical equation. We specify the physical state (alongwith allotropic state) of the substance in an equation. For example: C2H5OH(l) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(l); ∆rH = – 1367 kJ mol–1 The above equation describes the combustion of liquid ethanol at constant temperature and pressure. The negative sign of enthalpy change indicates that this is an exothermic reaction. It would be necessary to remember the following conventions regarding thermochemical equations. 1. The coefficients in a balanced thermochemical equation refer to the number of moles (never molecules) of reactants and products involved in the reaction. 2. The numerical value of ∆rH  refers to the number of moles of substances specified by an equation. Standard enthalpy change ∆rH will have units as kJ mol–1.

For example in CH4, ∆C–HH  is calculated as: ∆C–HH = ¼ (∆a H) = ¼ (1665 kJ mol–1) = 416 kJ mol–1 We find that mean C–H bond enthalpy in methane is 416 kJ/mol. It has been found that mean C–H bond enthalpies differ slightly from compound to compound, as in CH3CH2Cl, CH3NO2, etc., but it does not differ in a great deal*. Using Hess’s law, bond enthalpies can be calculated. Bond enthalpy values of some single and multiple bonds are

It is the heat withdrawn from the surroundings when additional solvent is added to the solution. The enthalpy of dilution of a solution is dependent on the original concentration of the solution and the amount of solvent added. 5.6 spontaneity The first law of thermodynamics tells us about the relationship between the heat absorbed and the work performed on or by a system. It puts no restrictions on the direction of heat flow. However, the flow of heat is unidirectional from higher temperature to lower temperature. In fact, all naturally occurring processes whether chemical or physical will tend to proceed spontaneously in one direction only. For example, a gas expanding to fill the available volume, burning carbon in dioxygen giving carbon dioxide. But heat will not flow from colder body to warmer body on its own, the gas in a container will not spontaneously contract into one corner or carbon dioxide will not form carbon and dioxygen spontaneously. These and many other spontaneously occurring changes show unidirectional change. We may ask ‘what is the driving force of spontaneously occurring changes ? What determines the direction of a spontaneous change ? In this section, we shall establish some criterion for these processes whether these will take place or not. Let us first understand what do we mean by spontaneous reaction or change ? You may think by your common observation that spontaneous reaction is one which occurs immediately when contact is made between the reactants. Take the case of combination of hydrogen and oxygen. These gases may be mixed at room temperature and left for

many years without observing any perceptible change. Although the reaction is taking place between them, it is at an extremely slow rate. It is still called spontaneous reaction. So spontaneity means ‘having the potential to proceed without the assistance of external agency’. However, it does not tell about the rate of the reaction or process. Another aspect of spontaneous reaction or process, as we see is that these cannot reverse their direction on their own. We may summarise it as follows: A spontaneous process is an irreversible process and may only be reversed by some external agency. (a) Is Decrease in Enthalpy a Criterion for Spontaneity ? If we examine the phenomenon like flow of water down hill or fall of a stone on to the ground, we find that there is a net decrease in potential energy in the direction of change. By analogy, we may be tempted to state that a chemical reaction is spontaneous in a given direction, because decrease in energy has taken place, as in the case of exothermic reactions. For example: N (g) + H2(g) = NH3(g); 2 2 ∆r H  = – 46.1 kJ mol–1 H (g) + Cl2(g) = HCl (g); 2 2 ∆r H  = – 92.32 kJ mol–1 H2(g) + O2(g) → H2O(l) ; ∆ H  = –285.8 kJ mol–1 r

The decrease in enthalpy in passing from reactants to products may be shown for any exothermic reaction on an enthalpy diagram as shown in Fig. 5.10(a). Thus, the postulate that driving force for a chemical reaction may be due to decrease in energy sounds ‘reasonable’ as the basis of evidence so far ! As far as a chemical reaction is concerned, this entropy change can be attributed to rearrangement of atoms or ions from one pattern in the reactants to another (in the products). If the structure of the products is very much disordered than that of the reactants, there will be a resultant increase in entropy. The change in entropy accompanying a chemical reaction may be estimated qualitatively by a consideration of the structures of the species taking part in the reaction. Decrease of regularity in structure would mean increase in entropy. For a given substance, the crystalline solid state is the state of lowest entropy (most ordered), The gaseous state is state of highest entropy. Now let us try to quantify entropy. One way to calculate the degree of disorder or chaotic distribution of energy among molecules would be through statistical method which is beyond the scope of this treatment. Other way would be to relate this process to the heat involved in a process which would make entropy a thermodynamic concept. Entropy, like any other thermodynamic property such as internal energy U and enthalpy H is a state function and ∆S is independent of path. Whenever heat is added to the system, it increases molecular motions causing increased randomness in the system. Thus heat (q) has randomising influence on the system. Can we then equate ∆S with q ? Wait ! Experience suggests us that the distribution of heat also depends on the temperature at which heat is added to the system. A system at higher temperature has greater randomness in it than one at lower temperature. Thus, temperature is the measure of average chaotic motion of particles in the system. paragraphs.text: Summary Thermodynamics deals with energy changes in chemical or physical processes and enables us to study these changes quantitatively and to make useful predictions. For these purposes, we divide the universe into the system and the surroundings. Chemical or physical processes lead to evolution or absorption of heat (q), part of which may be converted into work (w). These quantities are related through the first law of thermodynamics via ∆U = q + w. ∆U, change in internal energy, depends on initial and final states only and is a state function, whereas q and w depend on the path and are not the state functions. We follow sign conventions of q and w by giving the positive sign to these quantities when these are added to the system. We can measure the transfer of heat from one system to another which causes the change in temperature. The magnitude of rise in temperature depends on the heat capacity (C) of a substance. Therefore, heat absorbed or evolved is q = C∆T. Work can be measured by w = –pex∆V, in case of expansion of gases. Under reversible process, we can put pex = p for infinitesimal changes in the volume making wrev = – p dV. In this condition, we can use gas equation, pV = nRT. At constant volume, w = 0, then ∆U = qV , heat transfer at constant volume. But in study of chemical reactions, we usually have constant pressure. We define another state function enthalpy. Enthalpy change, ∆H = ∆U + ∆ngRT, can be found directly from the heat changes at constant pressure, ∆H = qp. There are varieties of enthalpy changes. Changes of phase such as melting, vaporization and sublimation usually occur at constant temperature and can be characterized by enthalpy changes which are always positive. Enthalpy of formation, combustion and other enthalpy changes can be calculated using Hess’s law. Enthalpy change for chemical reactions can be determined by

We define another state function, S, entropy for this purpose. Entropy is a measure of disorder or randomness. For a spontaneous change, total entropy change is positive. Therefore, for an isolated system, ∆U = 0, ∆S > 0, so entropy change distinguishes a spontaneous change, while energy change does not. questions.question: When a liquid is in equilibrium with its vapor in a closed container at a constant temperature, which of the following statements is true?
options: The process of evaporation stops completely.
The rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation.
The rate of evaporation is greater than the rate of condensation.
There is a continuous net evaporation of liquid.
questions.explanation: B is correct because at equilibrium, the macroscopic properties (like vapor pressure) become constant, but the processes continue at equal and opposite rates. The number of molecules leaving the liquid equals the number returning from the vapor. A is wrong because equilibrium is dynamic, not static, meaning molecular activity at the boundary continues. C is wrong because for equilibrium to be established, the forward (evaporation) and reverse (condensation) rates must be equal. D is wrong because a net evaporation rate would imply the system is not yet at equilibrium, and vapor pressure would be increasing.
questions.hint: Recall the characteristics of a physical equilibrium, specifically regarding the rates of opposing processes.
questions.ncertPara: Chemical equilibria are important in numerous biological and environmental processes. For example, equilibria involving O2 molecules and the protein hemoglobin play a crucial role in the transport and delivery of O2 from our lungs to our muscles. Similar equilibria involving CO molecules and hemoglobin account for the toxicity of CO. When a liquid evaporates in a closed container, molecules with relatively higher kinetic energy escape the liquid surface into the vapour phase and number of liquid molecules from the vapour phase strike the liquid surface and are retained in the liquid phase. It gives rise to a constant vapour pressure because of an equilibrium in which the number of molecules leaving the liquid equals the number returning to liquid from the vapour. We say that the system has reached equilibrium state at this stage. However, this is not static equilibrium and there is a lot of activity at the boundary between the liquid and the vapour. Thus, at equilibrium, the rate of evaporation is equal to the rate of condensation. It may be represented by H2O (l)

The reaction is carried out in an open container.
questions.explanation: A is correct because a characteristic feature of dynamic equilibrium is that the macroscopic properties, including the concentrations of reactants and products, stop changing and remain constant over time. B is wrong because concentrations become constant, but they are not necessarily equal. C is wrong because equilibrium is dynamic; reactions continue in both directions at equal rates, they do not stop. D is wrong because chemical equilibrium requires a closed system to prevent loss or gain of matter.

questions.question: Which statement accurately describes a system at dynamic chemical equilibrium?
options: No further change occurs at the molecular level, making the system static.
The concentrations of reactants continue to decrease slowly, while products increase.
The concentrations of all species remain constant because the rates of the forward and reverse processes are equal.
The rates of opposing processes are not necessarily equal, but the net change in concentration is zero.
questions.explanation: C is correct because at dynamic equilibrium, macroscopic properties like concentrations of reactants and products become constant, not because the reaction stops, but because the rate of the forward reaction becomes exactly equal to the rate of the reverse reaction. This leads to no net change in concentrations. A is wrong because at a molecular level, intense activity continues with molecules interconverting between reactants and products. B is wrong as concentrations become constant, not slowly decreasing. D is wrong because the equality of rates of opposing processes is a defining characteristic of dynamic equilibrium.
questions.hint: Recall that equilibrium is dynamic at the molecular level, yet stable at the macroscopic level.

Based on the extent to which the reactions proceed to reach the state of chemical equilibrium, these may be classified in three groups. (ii) The reactions in which only small amounts of products are formed and most of the reactants remain unchanged at equilibrium stage. (iii) The reactions in which the concentrations of the reactants and products are comparable, when the system is in equilibrium. The extent of a reaction in equilibrium varies with the experimental conditions such as concentrations of reactants, temperature, etc. Optimisation of the operational conditions is very important in industry and laboratory so that equilibrium is favorable in the direction of the desired product. questions.question: Consider a system of ice and water in a perfectly insulated thermos flask at 273 K and atmospheric pressure. Which statement correctly describes this solid-liquid equilibrium?
options: The system is static, meaning no molecular exchange occurs between ice and water.
The mass of ice gradually decreases while the mass of water increases until all ice melts.
Both ice and water continuously interconvert at equal rates, maintaining constant masses and temperature.
The temperature of the system continuously fluctuates around 273 K.
questions.explanation: C is correct. The text explicitly states that at equilibrium, both opposing processes (melting and freezing) occur simultaneously at the same rate, resulting in no change in the mass of ice and water, and the temperature remains constant. A is wrong because the equilibrium is dynamic, involving continuous molecular exchange. B is wrong because at equilibrium, the masses of ice and water remain constant, not changing in one direction. D is wrong because the temperature of the system remains constant at the normal melting point (273 K at 1 atm) during equilibrium.
questions.hint: Recall that physical equilibrium, like chemical equilibrium, is dynamic, not static.

questions.question: Based on the extent to which reactions proceed to reach chemical equilibrium, they are classified into three groups. Which of the following statements about these classifications is INCORRECT?
options: Some reactions proceed nearly to completion, leaving only negligible concentrations of reactants.
Some reactions form only small amounts of products, with most of the reactants remaining unchanged at equilibrium.
In one type of equilibrium, products are formed almost entirely, and reactant concentrations become comparable to products.
In another type, the concentrations of reactants and products are comparable when the system is in equilibrium.
questions.explanation: C is incorrect. The text describes three groups: (i) reactions that proceed nearly to completion (negligible reactants left), (ii) reactions forming small amounts of products (most reactants unchanged), and (iii) reactions where reactant and product concentrations are comparable. A reaction where products are formed almost entirely implies negligible reactants, so their concentrations cannot be 'comparable' to products. This statement incorrectly mixes the characteristics of group (i) and group (iii). A is correct (group i), B is correct (group ii), and D is correct (group iii).
questions.hint: Carefully distinguish between reactions that go 'nearly to completion' versus those where 'concentrations are comparable'.

questions.question: What is defined as the normal melting point of a pure substance?
options: The temperature at which a pure substance boils at atmospheric pressure.
The temperature at which a solid and liquid are in equilibrium at any pressure.
The temperature at which the solid and liquid phases of a pure substance are in equilibrium at atmospheric pressure.
The temperature and pressure at which all three phases (solid, liquid, gas) coexist in equilibrium.
questions.explanation: C is correct. The text explicitly defines 'normal melting point' (or normal freezing point) as the temperature at which the solid and liquid phases of any pure substance are at equilibrium at atmospheric pressure. A defines the normal boiling point. B is incorrect because 'normal' implies atmospheric pressure, not 'any pressure'. D defines the triple point, which is not discussed on this page and is distinct from the normal melting point.
questions.hint: Pay close attention to the conditions of pressure mentioned in the definition.
questions.ncertPara: characteristic features. We observe that the mass of ice and water do not change with time and the temperature remains constant. However, the equilibrium is not static. The intense activity can be noticed at the boundary between ice and water. Molecules from the liquid water collide against ice and adhere to it and some molecules of ice escape into liquid phase. There is no change of mass of ice and water, as the rates of transfer of molecules from ice into water and of reverse transfer from water into ice are equal at atmospheric pressure and 273 K. It is obvious that ice and water are in equilibrium only at particular temperature and pressure. For any pure substance at atmospheric pressure, the temperature at which the solid and liquid phases are at equilibrium is called the normal melting point or normal freezing point of the substance. The system here is in dynamic equilibrium and we can infer the following: Both the opposing processes occur (i) simultaneously. (ii) Both the processes occur at the same rate so that the amount of ice and water remains constant. 6.1.2 Liquid-Vapour Equilibrium This equilibrium can be better understood if we consider the example of a transparent box carrying a U-tube with mercury (manometer). Drying agent like anhydrous calcium chloride (or phosphorus penta-oxide) is placed for a few hours in the box. After removing the drying agent by tilting the box on one side, a watch glass (or petri dish) containing water is quickly placed inside the box. It will be observed that the mercury level in the right limb of the manometer slowly increases and finally attains a constant value, that is, the pressure inside the box increases and reaches a constant value. Also the volume of water in the watch glass decreases (Fig. 6.1). Initially there was no water vapour (or very less) inside the box. As water evaporated the pressure in the box increased due to addition of water molecules into the gaseous phase inside the box. The rate of evaporation is constant.

questions.question: A watch glass containing water is quickly placed inside a transparent closed box. Which observation correctly describes the process of achieving liquid-vapour equilibrium?
options: The rate of evaporation decreases as the pressure increases inside the box.
The pressure inside the box decreases as water evaporates from the watch glass.
The pressure inside the box increases until it becomes constant, and the volume of liquid water decreases until it becomes constant.
The volume of liquid water continuously increases due to condensation of water vapour.
questions.explanation: C is correct. The text states, 'the pressure inside the box increased due to addition of water molecules into the gaseous phase inside the box' and 'reaches a constant value'. It also mentions 'the volume of water in the watch glass decreases'. This decrease continues until equilibrium is established, at which point it becomes constant (assuming some liquid remains). A is wrong because the text states 'The rate of evaporation is constant' (referring to the intrinsic rate). B is wrong because the pressure increases due to vapor formation. D is wrong because the volume of liquid water decreases initially due to net evaporation.
questions.hint: Remember that the system is closed and the intrinsic rate of evaporation is constant, while the vapor pressure builds up.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly defines the equilibrium vapour pressure of a liquid?
options: The pressure exerted by the liquid phase on the walls of the container at a given temperature.
The constant pressure exerted by vapour molecules at a given temperature when liquid and vapour are in equilibrium in a closed system.
The total pressure of the gaseous mixture above a liquid, irrespective of equilibrium conditions.
The maximum pressure attained by the vapour phase just before condensation begins at a given temperature.
questions.explanation: B is correct because the equilibrium vapour pressure is defined as the pressure exerted by the vapour phase when it is in dynamic equilibrium with its liquid phase at a specific temperature. A is wrong because it refers to the pressure of the liquid itself, not the vapour. C is wrong because 'total pressure' could include other gases, whereas vapour pressure is specific to the substance's vapour. D is wrong because equilibrium vapour pressure is a property *at* equilibrium, not a transient pressure before condensation starts.
questions.hint: Recall the conditions under which 'equilibrium vapour pressure' is measured and what exactly contributes to this pressure.

All liquid molecules have converted into the vapour phase.
The rate of condensation of vapour into liquid becomes zero.
The rate of evaporation becomes equal to the rate of condensation.

B is wrong as complete conversion to vapour means no liquid is left, hence no equilibrium. C is wrong because condensation continues at equilibrium, balancing evaporation.

A liquid with higher equilibrium vapour pressure is more volatile and has a higher boiling point.
A liquid with higher equilibrium vapour pressure is more volatile and has a lower boiling point.
Equilibrium vapour pressure is independent of both volatility and boiling point.
questions.explanation: C is correct. A is wrong because higher vapour pressure implies higher volatility. B is wrong because higher vapour pressure leads to a lower boiling point. D is wrong because vapour pressure and boiling point are intrinsically related.

questions.question: When a liquid is exposed to the atmosphere in an open watch glass, why is it impossible for a liquid-vapour equilibrium to be established?
options: Vapour molecules disperse into the large volume of the room, making the rate of condensation much less than the rate of evaporation.
Equilibrium is eventually achieved if the initial volume of the liquid is very small.
The rate of evaporation eventually becomes zero due to the open nature of the system.
The rate of evaporation remains constant, preventing the establishment of a steady state.
questions.explanation: A is correct because, in an open system, vapour molecules continuously escape and disperse into the vast atmosphere, preventing the concentration of vapour from increasing sufficiently for the rate of condensation to match the rate of evaporation. This makes it impossible to achieve equilibrium. B is wrong as equilibrium cannot be reached in an open system. C is wrong; the liquid eventually disappears, and equilibrium is not established, regardless of the initial volume. D is wrong; while evaporation occurs, the key factor preventing equilibrium is the significantly lower rate of condensation due to dispersion.
questions.hint: Consider the fate of vapour molecules in an open system compared to a closed one.

questions.question: How does the boiling point of a pure liquid change when measured at a significantly higher altitude compared to sea level?
options: The boiling point increases.
The boiling point decreases.
The boiling point remains unchanged.
The rate of evaporation becomes constant at the higher altitude.
questions.explanation: B is correct. At higher altitudes, the atmospheric pressure is lower. Since the boiling point is the temperature at which the liquid's vapour pressure equals the external atmospheric pressure, a lower external pressure means the liquid will boil at a lower temperature. A is wrong because boiling point decreases at higher altitudes. C is wrong as boiling point is directly dependent on atmospheric pressure. D is wrong; while evaporation rates might be affected, the boiling point itself changes.

questions.question: A saturated solution of sugar in water at a constant temperature is prepared. If a small amount of radioactive sugar is added to this solution, which observation correctly describes the state of the system after some time?
options: No radioactivity is observed in the solution phase, only in the added solid sugar.
Radioactivity is only observed in the solution, and not in the original non-radioactive solid sugar.
The radioactive sugar remains as a separate layer and does not exchange with the non-radioactive sugar.
Radioactivity is observed in both the solid sugar and the sugar dissolved in the solution.
questions.explanation: D is correct because in a saturated solution, a dynamic equilibrium exists where the rate of dissolution of solid sugar equals the rate of crystallization of sugar. This means there is continuous exchange of molecules between the solid and solution phases. Adding radioactive sugar allows this exchange to be observed, as radioactive molecules will eventually appear in both phases. A is wrong because it describes a static equilibrium, which is not the case for dissolution. B is wrong because radioactivity will be observed in the solid phase due to crystallization of radioactive sugar from the solution. C is wrong because the exchange is continuous, leading to radioactivity in both phases.
questions.hint: Recall the characteristic nature of dynamic equilibrium in a saturated solution.
questions.ncertPara: 6.1.4 Equilibrium Involving Dissolution of Solid or Gases in Liquids Solids in liquids We know from our experience that we can dissolve only a limited amount of salt or sugar in a given amount of water at room temperature. If we make a thick sugar syrup solution by dissolving sugar at a higher temperature, sugar crystals separate out if we cool the syrup to the room temperature. We call it a saturated solution when no more of solute can be dissolved in it at a given temperature. The concentration of the solute in a saturated solution depends upon the temperature. In a saturated solution, a dynamic equilibrium exits between the solute molecules in the solid state and in the solution: Sugar (solid), and Sugar (solution) the rate of dissolution of sugar = rate of crystallisation of sugar. Equality of the two rates and dynamic nature of equilibrium has been confirmed with the help of radioactive sugar. If we drop some radioactive sugar into saturated solution of non-radioactive sugar, then after some time radioactivity is observed both in the solution and in the solid sugar. Initially there were no radioactive sugar molecules in the solution but due to dynamic nature of equilibrium, there is exchange between the radioactive and non-radioactive sugar molecules between the two phases. The ratio of the radioactive to non-radioactive molecules in the solution increases till it attains a constant value. Gases in liquids When a soda water bottle is opened, some of the carbon dioxide gas dissolved in it fizzes out rapidly. The phenomenon arises due to difference in solubility of carbon dioxide at different pressures. questions.question: Consider the dissolution of a solid in a liquid and a gas in a liquid. How does increasing the temperature typically affect their solubility?
options: Solubility of gases decreases, while solubility of most solids increases.
Solubility of gases increases, while solubility of most solids decreases.
Solubility of both gases and solids increases.
Solubility of both gases and solids decreases.
questions.explanation: A is correct because for gases dissolved in liquids, increasing temperature decreases their solubility as the increased kinetic energy of gas molecules allows them to escape the solution. For most solids, increasing temperature increases their solubility as it aids in breaking the solute-solute interactions and allows for greater solute-solvent interactions, though the text only states it 'depends on temperature' for solids, implying a typical increase, unlike the explicit decrease mentioned for gases. B is wrong as it reverses the effect for gases. C is wrong as it reverses the effect for solids. D is wrong because the effects are generally opposite for gases and solids.
questions.hint: Remember how kinetic energy affects gas molecules in solution versus the lattice energy of solids.

questions.question: According to Henry's law, for the dissolution of a gas in a liquid at a constant temperature, what is the relationship between the mass of the gas dissolved and the pressure of the gas above the solvent?
options: The mass of the gas dissolved is inversely proportional to the pressure of the gas above the solvent.
The mass of the gas dissolved is independent of the pressure of the gas above the solvent.
The mass of the gas dissolved remains constant regardless of the pressure changes.
The mass of the gas dissolved is directly proportional to the pressure of the gas above the solvent.
questions.explanation: D is correct as per Henry's law, which states that the mass of a gas dissolved in a given mass of a solvent at any temperature is proportional to the pressure of the gas above the solvent. A, B, and C describe incorrect relationships; the relationship is direct proportionality, not inverse or independent.
questions.hint: Recall the direct proportionality stated by Henry's law.

questions.question: When a soda water bottle is opened, carbon dioxide gas rapidly fizzes out. This phenomenon is best explained by:
options: A decrease in the partial pressure of $CO_{2}$ above the solution, causing dissolved $CO_{2}$ to escape to establish a new equilibrium based on Henry's law.
An increase in the pressure inside the bottle upon opening, forcing more $CO_{2}$ out.
An increase in the temperature of the solution after opening, which increases the solubility of $CO_{2}$.
The solubility of $CO_{2}$ in water significantly increases when the bottle is opened to the atmosphere.
questions.explanation: A is correct. The soda bottle is sealed under high pressure of $CO_{2}$. When opened, the external pressure drops to atmospheric pressure, significantly reducing the partial pressure of $CO_{2}$ above the solution. According to Henry's law, the solubility of $CO_{2}$ decreases with decreasing pressure, leading to the dissolved $CO_{2}$ escaping as gas until a new equilibrium is established. B is wrong; opening the bottle decreases pressure, not increases it. C is wrong; temperature generally decreases gas solubility, but the primary cause here is pressure change. D is wrong; solubility of $CO_{2}$ decreases, it does not increase upon opening.
questions.hint: Consider the state of the gas inside the sealed bottle and what happens when pressure changes.

questions.question: Which of the following statements accurately defines a saturated solution?
options: A solution that can still dissolve a significant amount of solute.
A solution containing more solute than normally possible, which will rapidly crystallize.
A solution in which no more solute can be dissolved at a given temperature.
A solution where solute dissolves rapidly without reaching a limit.
questions.explanation: C is correct. A saturated solution is defined as one where no more of the solute can be dissolved in it at a given temperature. This implies that the solution is in dynamic equilibrium with any undissolved solute. A is incorrect as it describes an unsaturated solution. B is incorrect as it implies an unstable state where crystallization would occur, possibly a supersaturated solution, which is not what 'saturated' primarily defines. D is incorrect as it describes an unsaturated solution, and the 'rapidly' part is irrelevant to the definition.
questions.hint: Focus on the maximum amount of solute that can be dissolved under specific conditions.

topic: Characteristics of Physical and Chemical Equilibrium

questions.question: For a physical process to attain equilibrium, which of the following conditions is mandatory?
options: The system must be closed, but temperature can fluctuate within a small range.
The system can be open, provided the temperature is strictly constant.
The system must be closed, and the temperature must be maintained constant.
The net rate of change of measurable properties must be non-zero until equilibrium.
questions.explanation: C is correct because the text explicitly states: 'Equilibrium is possible only in a closed system at a given temperature.' This means both a closed system and constant temperature are essential. A is incorrect because the temperature must be constant, not just fluctuating within a range. B is incorrect because equilibrium in physical processes requires a closed system. D is incorrect because at equilibrium, all measurable properties remain constant, implying a net rate of change of zero.
questions.hint: Recall the conditions specified for physical equilibria, particularly regarding system boundary and temperature control.
questions.ncertPara: 6.1.5 General Characteristics of Equilibria Involving Physical Processes For the physical processes discussed above, following characteristics are common to the system at equilibrium: (i) Equilibrium is possible only in a closed system at a given temperature. (ii) Both the opposing processes occur at the same rate and there is a dynamic but stable condition. (iii) All measurable properties of the system remain constant. (iv) When equilibrium is attained for a physical process, it is characterised by constant value of one of its parameters at a given temperature. Table 6.1 lists such quantities. (v) The magnitude of such quantities at any stage indicates the extent to which the physical process has proceeded before reaching equilibrium. 6.2

questions.question: Which statement best describes the nature of chemical equilibrium?
options: The forward and reverse reactions stop, leading to constant concentrations.
The forward and reverse reactions continue to occur at equal rates.
Reactant concentrations become zero at equilibrium.
Only the forward reaction proceeds at equilibrium, but at a very slow rate.
questions.explanation: B is correct. The text states, 'This equilibrium is dynamic in nature as it consists of a forward reaction... and reverse reaction in which product(s) gives the original reactants.' It also says, 'the rates of the forward and reverse reactions become equal.' A is incorrect because reactions do not stop; they continue at equal rates. C is incorrect as reactant concentrations remain constant, not necessarily zero, at equilibrium. D is incorrect because both forward and reverse reactions occur at equilibrium.
questions.hint: Remember that chemical equilibrium is 'dynamic' in nature.
questions.ncertPara: EQUILIBRIUM IN CHEMICAL PROCESSES – DYNAMIC EQUILIBRIUM Analogous to the physical systems chemical reactions also attain a state of equilibrium. These reactions can occur both in forward and backward directions. When the rates of the forward and reverse reactions become equal, the concentrations of the reactants and the products remain constant. This is the stage of chemical equilibrium. This equilibrium is dynamic in nature as it consists of a forward reaction in which the reactants give product(s) and reverse reaction in which product(s) gives the original reactants. For a better comprehension, let us consider a general case of a reversible reaction, A+B

questions.question: Upon reaching equilibrium in a physical process, which statement accurately describes the system's measurable properties?
options: They fluctuate slightly around a steady average value due to microscopic activity.
They change continuously until one reactant is completely consumed.
They remain constant, and this constancy is often characterized by a specific parameter's constant value at a given temperature.
They stop changing because all molecular motion ceases.

questions.question: A reversible chemical reaction, $A + B \rightleftharpoons C + D$, is allowed to reach equilibrium. Which statement regarding the initial conditions for reaching this equilibrium is correct?
options: Equilibrium can only be reached if starting with A and B.
Equilibrium can only be reached if starting with C and D.
Equilibrium can be reached by starting with A and B, or with C and D, or a mixture of all four.
Equilibrium is reached when all reactants are consumed.
questions.explanation: C is correct. The text explicitly states, 'the reaction can reach the state of equilibrium even if we start with only C and D; that is, no A and B being present initially, as the equilibrium can be reached from either direction.' This implies starting with reactants, products, or a mixture of both can lead to the same equilibrium state. A and B are incorrect because equilibrium can be reached from either direction. D is incorrect as equilibrium is a state where concentrations become constant, not where reactants are fully consumed.
questions.hint: Consider whether equilibrium is a state achievable only from reactants or also from products.

paragraphs.text: Dynamic Equilibrium – A Student’s Activity Equilibrium whether in a physical or in a chemical system, is always of dynamic nature. This can be demonstrated by the use of radioactive isotopes. This is not feasible in a school laboratory. However this concept can be easily comprehended by performing the following activity. The activity can be performed in a group of 5 or 6 students. Take two 100mL measuring cylinders (marked as 1 and 2) and two glass tubes each of 30 cm length. Diameter of the tubes may be same or different in the range of 3-5mm. Fill nearly half of the measuring cylinder-1 with coloured water (for this purpose add a crystal of potassium permanganate to water) and keep second cylinder (number 2) empty. Put one tube in cylinder 1 and second in cylinder 2. Immerse one tube in cylinder 1, close its upper tip with a finger and transfer the coloured water contained in its lower portion to cylinder 2. Using second tube, kept in 2nd cylinder, transfer the coloured water in a similar manner from cylinder 2 to cylinder 1. In this way keep on transferring coloured water using the two glass tubes from cylinder 1 to 2 and from 2 to 1 till you notice that the level of coloured water in both the cylinders becomes constant. If you continue intertransferring coloured solution between the cylinders, there will not be any further change in the levels of coloured water in two cylinders. If we take analogy of ‘level’ of coloured water with ‘concentration’ of reactants and products in the two cylinders, we can say the process of transfer, which continues even after the constancy of level, is indicative of dynamic nature of the process. If we repeat the experiment taking two tubes of different diameters we find that at equilibrium the level of coloured water in two cylinders is different. How far diameters are responsible for change in levels in two cylinders? Empty cylinder (2) is an indicator of no product in it at the beginning.
Demonstrating dynamic nature of equilibrium. (a) initial stage (b) final stage after the equilibrium is attained.

paragraphs.text: Depiction of equilibrium for the reaction

equilibrium is attained, these two mixtures (H 2, N 2, NH 3 and D 2, N 2, ND 3) are mixed together and left for a while. Later, when this mixture is analysed, it is found that the concentration of ammonia is just the same as before. However, when this mixture is analysed by a mass spectrometer, it is found that ammonia and all deuterium containing forms of ammonia (NH3, NH2D, NHD2 and ND3) and dihydrogen and its deutrated forms (H2, HD and D2) are present. Thus one can conclude that scrambling of H and D atoms in the molecules must result from a continuation of the forward and reverse reactions in the mixture. If the reaction had simply stopped when they reached equilibrium, then there would have been no mixing of isotopes in this way. Use of isotope (deuterium) in the formation of ammonia clearly indicates that chemical reactions reach a state of dynamic equilibrium in which the rates of forward and reverse reactions are equal and there is no net change in composition. Equilibrium can be attained from both sides, whether we start reaction by taking, H2(g) and N2(g) and get NH3(g) or by taking NH3(g) and decomposing it into N2(g) and H2(g). N2(g) + 3H2(g)

Similarly let us consider the reaction, 2HI(g). If we start with H 2 (g) + I 2 (g) equal initial concentration of H2 and I2, the reaction proceeds in the forward direction and the concentration of H2 and I2 decreases while that of HI increases, until all of these become constant at equilibrium (Fig. 6.5). We can also start with HI alone and make the reaction to proceed in the reverse direction; the concentration of HI will decrease and concentration of H2 and I2 will increase until they all become constant when equilibrium is reached (Fig. 6.5). If total number of H and I atoms are same in a given volume, the same equilibrium mixture is obtained whether we start it from pure reactants or pure product.
Fig. 6.5 Chemical equilibrium in the reaction H2(g) + I2(g) 2HI(g) can be attained from either direction

The equilibrium constant for a general reaction, aA + bB
is expressed as, Kc = [C]c[D]d / [A]a[B]b

where [A], [B], [C] and [D] are the equilibrium concentrations of the reactants and products. Equilibrium constant for the reaction, 4NO(g) + 6H2O(g) is written 4NH3(g) + 5O2(g) as Kc = [NO]4[H2O]6 / [NH3]4 [O2]5 is far from constant. However, if we consider the expression, [HI(g)]2eq / [H2(g)]eq [I2(g)]eq we find that this expression gives constant value (as shown in Table 6.3) in all the six cases. It can be seen that in this expression the power of the concentration for reactants and products are actually the stoichiometric coefficients in the equation for the chemical reaction. If Qc = Kc, the reaction mixture is already at equilibrium. Consider the gaseous reaction of H 2 with I2, H2(g) + I2(g) 2HI(g); Kc = 57.0 at 700 K. Suppose we have molar concentrations [H2]t=0.10M, [I2]t = 0.20 M and [HI]t = 0.40 M. (the subscript t on the concentration symbols means that the concentrations were measured at some arbitrary time t, not necessarily at equilibrium). Thus, the reaction quotient, Qc at this stage of the reaction is given by, Qc = [HI]t2 / [H2]t [I2]t = (0.40)2/ (0.10)×(0.20) = 8.0 Now, in this case, Qc (8.0) does not equal Kc (57.0), so the mixture of H2(g), I2(g) and HI(g) is not at equilibrium; that is, more H2(g) and I2(g) will react to form more HI(g) and their concentrations will decrease till Qc = Kc. paragraphs.text: reactants to products while minimising the expenditure of energy. This implies maximum yield of products at mild temperature and pressure conditions. If it does not happen, then the experimental conditions need to be adjusted. For example, in the Haber process for the synthesis of ammonia from N2 and H2, the choice of experimental conditions is of real economic importance. Annual world production of ammonia is about hundred million tones, primarily for use as fertilisers. Equilibrium constant, Kc is independent of initial concentrations. But if a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in the concentration of one or more of the reacting substances, then the system is no longer at equilibrium; and net reaction takes place in some direction until the system returns to equilibrium once again. Similarly, a change in temperature or pressure of the system may also alter the equilibrium. In order to decide what course the reaction adopts and make a qualitative prediction about the effect of a change in conditions on equilibrium we use Le Chatelier’s principle. It states that a change in any of the factors that determine the equilibrium conditions of a system will cause the system to change in such a manner so as to reduce or to counteract the effect of the change. This is applicable to all physical and chemical equilibria.

“When the concentration of any of the reactants or products in a reaction at equilibrium is changed, the composition of the equilibrium mixture changes so as to minimize the effect of concentration changes”. Let us take the reaction, H2(g) + I2(g)

If H2 is added to the reaction mixture at equilibrium, then the equilibrium of the reaction is disturbed. In order to restore it, the reaction proceeds in a direction wherein H2 is consumed, i.e., more of H2 and I2 react to form HI and finally the equilibrium shifts in right (forward) direction (Fig.6.8). This is in accordance with the Le Chatelier’s principle which implies that in case of addition of a reactant/product, a new equilibrium will be set up in which the concentration of the reactant/product should be less than what it was after the addition but more than what it was in the original mixture.

Similarly, we can say that removal of a product also boosts the forward reaction and increases the concentration of the products and this has great commercial application in cases of reactions, where the product is a gas or a volatile substance. In case of manufacture of ammonia, ammonia is liquified and removed from the reaction mixture so that reaction keeps moving in forward direction. Similarly, in the large scale production of CaO (used as important building material) from CaCO3, constant removal of CO2 from the kiln drives the reaction to completion. It should be remembered that continuous removal of a product maintains Qc at a value less than Kc and reaction continues to move in the forward direction. Hydrochloric acid present in the gastric juice is secreted by the lining of our stomach in a significant amount of 1.2-1.5 L/day and is essential for digestive processes. The extent to which ionization occurs depends upon the strength of the bond and the extent of solvation of ions produced. The terms dissociation and ionization have earlier been used with different meaning. Dissociation refers to the process of separation of ions in water already existing as such in the solid state of the solute, as in sodium chloride. On the other hand, ionization corresponds to a process in which a neutral molecule splits into charged ions in the solution. Here, we shall not distinguish between the two and use the two terms interchangeably.

Hydronium and Hydroxyl Ions Hydrogen ion by itself is a bare proton with very small size (~10–15 m radius) and intense electric field, binds itself with the water molecule at one of the two available lone pairs on it giving H3O+. This species has been detected in many compounds (e.g., H3O+Cl–) in the solid state. In aqueous solution the hydronium ion is further hydrated to give species like H5O2+, H7O3+ and H9O4+. Similarly the hydroxyl ion is hydrated to give several ionic species like H3O2–, H5O3– and H7O4– etc.

6.10.1 Arrhenius Concept of Acids and Bases According to Arrhenius theory, acids are substances that dissociates in water to give hydrogen ions H +(aq) and bases are substances that produce hydroxyl ions OH –(aq). The ionization of an acid HX (aq) can be represented by the following equations: HX (aq) → H+(aq) + X– (aq) or HX(aq) + H2O(l) → H3O+(aq) + X –(aq) A bare proton, H+ is very reactive and cannot exist freely in aqueous solutions. Thus, it bonds to the oxygen atom of a solvent water molecule to give trigonal pyramidal hydronium ion, H3O+ {[H (H2O)]+} (see box). In this chapter we shall use H+(aq) and H3O+(aq) interchangeably to mean the same i.e., a hydrated proton.
